result:
I have a small, stubborn habit that has annoyed everyone who has ever tried to meet me for coffee. I am always late, and not because I am disorganized or because the bus was late or because I stopped to buy something I did not need, though all of those things have happened. I am late because I take the long way. Not the scenic way, exactly, because I do not always know what is scenic. I just turn left when I could turn right. I cut through a park when the street would be faster. I follow a canal because the water looks thoughtful. It is a minor rebellion, mostly harmless, and it has taught me more about the cities I live in than any map ever has.

There is a particular dignity to the direct route that I admire in other people. They have places to be. They have calibrated their lives to the green pedestrian light and the shortest line between two points. I admire them the way I admire people who can fold a fitted sheet, with a sort of fascinated horror. I cannot do it. My feet seem to have their own opinions. When I am tired I walk faster and straighter, head down, mission-oriented. But when I am not tired, which is perhaps the only time I truly need to arrive anywhere worth arriving, I drift. I into shop windows I have no intention of entering. I read plaques. I watch pigeons negotiate peace over a dropped crust. These are not detours in the old sense of mileage. They are detours in attention.

The long way home was how I learned my neighborhood as a child, though I did not think of it as learning then. I thought of it as avoiding. There was a house on our street with a dog who considered his fence a suggestion and his bark a full legal argument. I would cross to the other side, then second-guess, then cross back, until my route home from school sprawled across three streets that did not need to be involved. My mother called it dawdling. She was right, but dawdling is a precise word. To dawdle is to move slowly and purposelessly, and purposelessness, I have come to believe, is a skill we train out of children with alarming efficiency. We praise them for being on task, on time, on track, as if a life were a train schedule.

As adults we are told to optimize. Optimize your commute. Optimize your morning routine. Optimize your sleep. Optimization is not a bad thing in itself; a surgeon should optimize, a pilot should optimize, a person trying to get to the emergency room should absolutely optimize. But a walker is not a surgeon, and a Tuesday afternoon is not an emergency, and yet we apply the logic of the operating theater to everything. We sprint through parks to get to our desks. We listen to podcasts at one and a half speed so we can consume more information while moving through space that was never meant to be consumed. I wonder if we are optimizing ourselves out of the very experience we were trying to reach.

Last October I walked home from work by a route I had never taken, mostly because it was raining and my usual underpass had flooded. I turned into a side street lined with brick buildings that sweated in the damp. The rain was not dramatic. It was the kind of steady, incurious rain that makes everything sound softer. Someone had left a crate of damp plums outside a grocery, and they glowed purple, absurdly beautiful against the gray. An old man was fixing a bicycle under an awning, swearing quietly at a chain that would not behave. A window on the second floor was open, and I could hear a woman practicing the same four bars of piano, over and over, with the patience of saints. None of this got me home faster. All of it got me home differently.

There is a Latin word, errare, that means both to wander and to make a mistake. The English word error comes from it, and so does errant, as in a knight errant, someone who wanders in search of adventure. I love that double meaning. To err is to miss the mark, to wander off the path. To be errant is to leave the path on purpose, or at least with a certain romance. We have kept the judgment and mostly lost the romance. We call a wandering mind unfocused, as if focus were always a virtue and wandering always a failure. But sometimes the mind wanders because the straight line has been walked too many times. It wanders because it is looking for the crate of plums, the bicycle repair, the piano bars. It is not broken. It is browsing.

The irony, of course, is that the long way often turns out to be the short way in memory. I can recite the direct route from my office to my apartment in three turns, and I remember none of it. The long way, the flooded underpass, the plums, the man swearing at his bicycle, I will remember that walk when the direct one is completely erased. This is true of conversations as well, and of books, and of friendships. The efficient version is forgettable. The meandering version is where the texture lives. We like to say that time flies, but I think time walks, and it walks the long way. It lingers in doorways. It stops to read the plaque. It buys fruit it does not need because the fruit, for a second, looked like a small, purple affirmation of beauty.

So tomorrow, when I am late again, forgive me. I am not lost. I am practicing an older art, one that predates GPS and deadlines and the moral panic about wasted minutes. I am taking the long way home, and in doing so I am arriving home on time in the only sense that ever really mattered to me, which is that I arrived having actually been somewhere.
